content: The principal investigators of the STREAM trial presented the preliminary findings of their study at the 48th Union World Conference on Lung Health. The trial enrolled patients between July 2012 and June 2015 in Ethiopia, Mongolia, South Africa, and Vietnam. The intention-to-treat (ITT) population included 424 participants (282 in the study arm and 142 in the control arm), while the modified ITT (mITT) population included 369 participants (245 in the study arm and 124 in the control arm). Treatment allocation was not blinded to participants, caregivers, or data managers, but all laboratory assessments, including microbiological tests used to determine patient outcomes, were conducted in a blinded manner. Audiometry was available at only one site. When the preliminary data were presented, the findings sparked public debate and raised questions about the implications of continuing the regimen under programmatic conditions, particularly among people living with HIV (PLHIV), where mortality was higher in the study arm compared to the control arm. Based on these preliminary results, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a position statement recommending the continued use of the shorter multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimen until a full update of the MDR-TB treatment guidelines was completed later that year. In July 2018, the final results of the STREAM trial were made available to WHO. The trial demonstrated the non-inferiority of the shorter regimen compared to the longer, conventional regimens described in the 2011 and 2016 WHO treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis. The shorter regimen, lasting 9–12 months, showed better adherence rates than the longer regimen, likely due to its reduced duration. However, direct comparisons between the shorter regimen and an all-oral longer regimen remain limited, as the longer regimens were typically reserved for patients ineligible for the shorter regimen. No data were reported to WHO on variants of the shorter regimen where the injectable agent was replaced by bedaquiline during the preparation of the 2018 guidelines. The 2018 recommendations emphasized the importance of excluding resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents before considering the shorter regimen. Additional testing, such as drug susceptibility testing (DST) for pyrazinamide and genotyping studies for isoniazid resistance, was also deemed important and should be performed if possible. For PLHIV, one-third of the STREAM trial participants were HIV-positive, and participation was not restricted by CD4 count. Among the 151 HIV-positive participants, 19 of the 24 deaths occurred at two sites in South Africa. The reasons for the higher mortality observed in the study arm among PLHIV remain unclear but may represent a clinically relevant signal. A detailed assessment of the causes of death by an expert panel did not indicate that the shorter regimen was associated with additional harms in PLHIV due to excessive pill burden, poor adherence, or drug–drug interactions with antiretroviral therapy (ART). The shorter regimen may be used in PLHIV alongside timely initiation of ART, careful monitoring of ART effectiveness, and management of adverse reactions. Prophylactic medication for opportunistic infections, adherence support, and close monitoring should also be part of routine HIV care. For patients with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) without confirmed isoniazid resistance, the shorter MDR-TB regimen may be used, provided other eligibility criteria are met. However, the STREAM trial demonstrated that baseline resistance to pyrazinamide and ethionamide was associated with a higher risk of treatment failure and relapse. In areas with high prevalence of resistance to these drugs, alternative regimens should be considered. Children were excluded from the STREAM trial, but 78 patients aged 18 years or younger were included in the 2018 individual patient data meta-analysis (IPD-MA) for the shorter regimen. While there is no biological reason to believe the regimen is less effective or tolerable in children, additional data on its use in this population would be valuable. Avoiding injectable agents in children is particularly desirable due to the risk of hearing loss, which can impact development. Children with pulmonary MDR/RR-TB should otherwise be considered for the shorter regimen under the same criteria as adults. Pregnancy was an exclusion criterion for the STREAM trial. Two components of the shorter regimen—injectable agents and ethionamide (or prothionamide)—are usually contraindicated in pregnancy. Withholding these medicines could compromise the regimen's effectiveness. For pregnant women, an individualized, longer regimen with four or more effective medicines and lower teratogenic risk is recommended. The findings from the STREAM trial were limited to patients with pulmonary TB and cannot be directly extrapolated to all forms of extrapulmonary disease. The shorter regimen should be avoided in patients with disseminated or central nervous system (CNS) TB, as well as in PLHIV with extrapulmonary disease. There are no specific data on the use of the shorter regimen in patients with diabetes mellitus. However, these patients should be given the same consideration for treatment with the shorter regimen as other patients, provided eligibility criteria are met. The shorter MDR-TB regimen has been widely adopted in the TB community due to its standardized composition and duration, making it relatively easy to implement. To replicate the high cure rates achieved in the STREAM trial, careful patient selection and effective support to ensure full adherence are essential. Testing for susceptibility or resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents should be conducted before starting the shorter regimen. Patients with strains resistant to these medicines should be transitioned to a longer regimen. Rapid and reliable DST for other regimen components, such as pyrazinamide, is also desirable. In settings where DST capacity is limited, decisions should be informed by clinical history and representative surveillance data. The shorter regimen may be initiated while awaiting test results, with the option to switch to a longer regimen if additional resistance is detected. The evidence for the effectiveness and safety of the shorter MDR-TB regimen now comes from both trial sites and observational studies conducted under standardized conditions. This evidence supports its use in eligible patients, but careful monitoring and adherence support remain critical to its success.
